title: The Financial Expert
description: Narayan's sixth novel, published by Methuen in London in 1952 and by Michigan State College Press in 1953. It tells the rise and fall of Margayya, who begins as a petty money-lender under a banyan tree outside the Central Co-operative Land Mortgage Bank in Malgudi, grows rich first by publishing a sex manual and then by taking deposits at extravagant interest, and is ruined by a run on his business. Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia calls it arguably one of Narayan's best and most popular novels, and William Walsh praised its 'intricate and silken organization'.
plot_or_argument:
Margayya does business under a banyan tree in front of the Central Co-operative Land Mortgage Bank in Malgudi: he helps the bank's shareholders borrow at low interest and lends the money to the needy at a higher rate, keeping the difference. The bank's Secretary and its peon, Arul Doss, seize the loan forms from his box and threaten to proceed against him, which sets him on the way to improving his position. Then his spoilt son, Balu, throws the red account book holding all his transactions into the gutter, and the old business cannot go on. An astrologer assures him that good times will come if he worships Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth, and he performs the worship for forty days, with ash from a red lotus and ghee from the milk of a grey cow. Soon afterwards Dr Pal sells him, for whatever cash is in his purse, the manuscript of a book on 'Bed Life'; Madan Lal, 'a man from the North', publishes it on equal shares as Domestic Harmony, it sells in great numbers, and Margayya makes his fortune.

His next ruin comes through Balu. Margayya enrols him in school in style, becomes secretary of the school committee and hires a tutor with orders to beat the boy when necessary, but Balu fails the school-leaving examination, tears up his certificate book, throws it into the same gutter and runs away. A letter from Madras reports him dead; Margayya, helped by a fellow traveller who is a plain-clothes police inspector, finds him alive and brings him home. He arranges Balu's marriage to Brinda, daughter of a tea-estate owner in the hills, dismissing an honest pundit who finds the horoscopes unmatched and paying another astrologer, found by Dr Pal, to certify that they agree, and he sets the couple up in Lawley Extension. To draw Dr Pal away from his son, he employs him to bring in deposits from black marketeers on the promise of high interest, paid out of the stream of new deposits. Margayya becomes rich, buys a car, stuffs every corner of his house with sacks of notes and gives to the War Fund when pressed.

One day he visits Balu's house, where Brinda, with her child, tells him in tears of her husband's nights; Balu then drives up with Dr Pal and two women of the town. Margayya drags Dr Pal from the car, beats him and sends the women away. The next day the bandaged Dr Pal whispers that Margayya's affairs are unsound; depositors besiege him, his wealth is paid out, hundreds remain unpaid, and he files for insolvency. In the end he tells Balu to take his old place under the banyan tree with the box, and when the young man hesitates, ashamed of what people will say, Margayya offers to go back there himself.
narrative_structure: A double cycle of rise and fall, each turn set off by Balu: the account book thrown into the gutter ends the first trade, and the certificate thrown into the same gutter begins the crisis that leads to the second. Gale observes that Narayan alternates the details of everyday Malgudi life with views into Margayya's mind, and Walsh praises 'a scheme of composition holding everything together in a vibrant and balanced union'. The ending returns Margayya to the banyan tree where he began.
principal_characters: Margayya; Meenakshi; Balu; Dr Pal; Madan Lal; Arul Doss; Brinda
meter_and_prosody: Narration that is, in Gale's words, 'serious and comic throughout', moving between the bank steps, the household and Margayya's private calculations. The comedy is gentle rather than satirical: his schemes, his rituals for Lakshmi and Dr Pal's patter are treated with irony but without contempt, in the plain, measured English Walsh found 'limpid, simple, calm and unaffected' (Contemporary Authors).
historical_context: Published in 1952 and set during the Second World War: Margayya gives to the War Fund, and his depositors are black marketeers, so the boom he exploits is the wartime economy of shortage and illicit profit (Wikipedia; Gale). The co-operative land-mortgage bank, an institution meant to give landholders cheap credit (general knowledge), supplies the margin he lives on. Methuen published it in London (as Mondal also notes), and the American edition of 1953 was one of several Narayan novels issued by Michigan State College Press in the 1950s.
literary_significance: Often counted among Narayan's finest novels: Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia calls it arguably one of his best and most popular, and cites the praise for it and for The Guide as typical of the response to his work. Gale singles out its portraits of Margayya, Dr Pal, Margayya's long-suffering wife Meenakshi and the prodigal Balu. The excerpt in Contemporary Literary Criticism reads it with The Vendor of Sweets as one of the novels told from a father's point of view, and G. S. Amur's essay on symbolism reads it with The English Teacher and The Vendor of Sweets. It was filmed in Kannada as Banker Margayya (1983) (Wikipedia).
bibliographical_notes: London: Methuen, 1952; East Lansing: Michigan State College Press, 1953 (Contemporary Authors). Filmed in Kannada as Banker Margayya (1983).
thematic_analysis: Money is the subject: Wikipedia calls the theme lust for money, and an excerpt reprinted in Contemporary Literary Criticism quotes Margayya's credo, 'Money alone is important in this world.' Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia reads the plot as a study of 'the vanity of human wishes', yet Margayya is no monster: Narayan keeps him human and able to hold the reader's sympathy (Wikipedia; Gale). Fathers and sons: the same excerpt pairs the book with The Vendor of Sweets as novels told from the father's side, and the spoilt, prodigal Balu, whom Margayya both indulges and has beaten, undoes him twice. Religion and fortune: worship of Lakshmi, horoscopes bought to order and astrology turned to business show piety entangled with greed. Society: Gale sets the rise and fall against wartime poverty, corruption, bureaucracy and the opportunism of businessmen and officials, while Dr Pal, 'the archetypal confidence man', embodies the town's appetite for easy money and illicit pleasure.
summary: Margayya helps the bank's shareholders borrow cheaply and relends the money at higher interest, until bank officials confiscate his forms and his spoilt son Balu throws his account book into a gutter. After forty days' worship of Lakshmi he buys from the shady Dr Pal a manuscript on 'Bed Life', which becomes the best-seller Domestic Harmony. He then grows rich on deposits brought in by Dr Pal from black marketeers, until his quarrel with Dr Pal over Balu's dissipation starts the run that bankrupts him and sends him back to the banyan tree.
critical_context: Walsh: the novel 'has an intricate and silken organization, a scheme of composition holding everything together in a vibrant and balanced union' (quoted by Gale). Gale's encyclopedia praises Narayan's 'powerful handling of the central theme of the vanity of human wishes and his deft manipulation of plot', and finds Margayya 'deeply flawed but also capable of retaining the reader's sympathy'. Amur's essay, reprinted in Contemporary Literary Criticism, traces the lotus pond, the garden and the ruined temple as symbols in this novel and two others.
research_notes: Not read. The plot follows Wikipedia's long summary, which is flagged as overlong but agrees with Gale's characterisation. Wikipedia puts the tea estate in the 'Memphis Hills', evidently Narayan's Mempi Hills, and gives a figure of 29 per cent for the promised interest; neither detail is used. Meenakshi's name comes from Gale.

title: Waiting for the Mahatma
description: Narayan's seventh novel, published in 1955 by Michigan State College Press (Contemporary Authors), with a London edition from Methuen (Mondal). Set in Malgudi in the last years of British rule, it follows Sriram, drawn into Gandhi's movement by his love for Bharati, and is unusual among Narayan's novels in bringing Gandhi on stage. Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia calls it his most political novel.
plot_or_argument: Sriram, who has finished high school, lives with his grandmother in Malgudi. He is attracted to Bharati, a girl of his own age who is active in Gandhi's Quit India movement, and becomes an activist himself. He then falls in with anti-British extremists, to his grandmother's great grief. His underground work takes him into a countryside that is alien to him, and his misunderstandings with the villagers provide, in Wikipedia's judgement, the book's best comic moments. After a spell in jail he is reunited with Bharati, and the novel ends with their engagement amid the tragedy of partition in 1947 and Gandhi's death in 1948. Gandhi appears as a character, and his ideas and practices are set against the views of traditionalists such as the town's notables and Sriram's grandmother. The romance is unconventional and is concluded outside either family's circle (Wikipedia); the women's studies article sees Bharati as Narayan's exemplary modern woman, graceful, disciplined, devoted to her teacher and to the nation.
narrative_structure: A chronological narrative that moves from the town to the countryside and to jail and closes on partition and Gandhi's death; the political struggle serves as the background to the romance (Wikipedia).
principal_characters: Sriram; Bharati; Sriram's grandmother; Mahatma Gandhi
meter_and_prosody: Narayan's 'gentle comic style' (Wikipedia), in low-key storytelling behind which, in the same article's phrase, much happens; the comedy of Sriram's encounters with villagers sits beside the gravity of Gandhi's scenes.
historical_context: Written in the early 1950s about the years from the Quit India movement, launched in August 1942, to independence and partition in 1947 and Gandhi's assassination in January 1948 (general historical dates). Michigan State College Press, which brought out Narayan's novels in America in the 1950s, published it in 1955.
literary_significance: Unusual among Narayan's novels in having Gandhi as a character and the independence struggle as its subject; Gale calls it his most political novel. Its politics have divided critics: vanden Driesen called it Narayan's neglected novel, and Richard Cronin's essay 'Quite Quiet India' uses it, with The Painter of Signs, to examine V. S. Naipaul's appraisal of the religious and the political in Narayan's work (eNotes).
bibliographical_notes: East Lansing: Michigan State College Press, 1955 (Contemporary Authors; Wikipedia's infobox names Michigan State University Press, the same press under its later name); London: Methuen (Mondal; year not given there).
thematic_analysis: Love and politics: Bharati draws Sriram into the national movement, and Cynthia vanden Driesen's essay traces his relationship to Gandhi (eNotes contents). Ambivalence towards nationalism: Satish Aikant (Journal of Commonwealth Literature, 2007) finds a 'colonial ambivalence', perhaps owed to Narayan's largely British readership, and Harveen Mann (ARIEL, 2000) a patriarchal nationalism (both cited by Wikipedia). Tradition against reform: Gandhi's practice against the grandmother and the notables. Women's agency: the women's studies article finds romantic and political purpose united in Bharati.
summary: Sriram, a high-school graduate living with his grandmother, follows Bharati into the Quit India movement, drifts into the company of anti-British extremists, is jailed, and is finally engaged to Bharati amid partition and the death of Gandhi.
research_notes: Not read. The plot is Wikipedia's (a stub with two scholarly references). The names of the extremist leader and other characters, found only in reader summaries, are not used. The date of the London edition was not checked.

title: The Guide
description: Narayan's best-known novel, published in New York by Viking and in London by Methuen in 1958. It tells how Raju, a tourist guide in Malgudi, becomes the lover and manager of a dancer, Rosie, goes to prison for forgery and, on his release, is taken for a holy man by villagers who expect him to fast to end a drought. It won the first Sahitya Akademi Award given to a book in English (1960), was filmed as Guide (1965) and staged in New York (1968), and Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia says it is usually considered Narayan's most accomplished novel.
plot_or_argument:
The novel begins after Raju's release from prison, with a villager, Velan, consulting him as a holy man at an abandoned temple near the village of Mangal. Brians's study guide notes the abrupt turns of the opening chapter, into the past and forward to the time when Raju will tell Velan his life story; from then on the narrative alternates between the present at the temple and the story of how Raju came there.

That story begins with 'Railway Raju', a popular and not very scrupulous guide to the sights around Malgudi. Among his clients are Marco, an archaeologist, and his wife Rosie, who longs to dance; Marco disapproves of her passion, but Raju encourages her to pursue it, and the two become close. When Marco learns of their relationship, he leaves Rosie in Malgudi and returns to Madras alone. Rosie takes refuge in Raju's home, and they live together; Raju's mother, who does not approve, leaves them. Raju becomes Rosie's stage manager, and through his promotion she wins recognition as a dancer. Success makes him overconfident; he asserts more and more control over her life for financial gain, becomes involved in a forgery case connected with Rosie's signature, and despite Rosie's defence is sentenced to two years in prison.

After his sentence Raju passes through Mangal and, rather than return to Malgudi in disgrace, stays in the temple and accepts the part the villagers give him, delivering sermons and settling their quarrels. When drought brings famine, some of the villagers come to believe that the rains will come if he fasts. Raju confesses his whole past to Velan, but Velan's faith is unchanged, and Raju resolves to go on with the fast. As news of it spreads through the press, a large crowd gathers to watch, to his annoyance. On the morning of the eleventh day he goes down to the river for his daily ritual, senses rain falling in the distant hills, and collapses into the water. Whether it really rained, and whether Raju died, the novel does not say.
narrative_structure: Two interleaved time-lines, the present at the temple near Mangal and Raju's past, with blank lines marking the shifts (Brians). The present is narrated in the third person and the past largely in Raju's own voice as he recounts it (general knowledge, not checked in the sources). The past catches up with the present at the fast, and the ending, on the eleventh day, is left open.
principal_characters: Raju; Rosie; Marco; Velan; Raju's mother
meter_and_prosody: Narayan's even, understated English carries both the comedy of Raju's opportunism and the gravity of the fast, and the ending refuses to decide between them. The vocabulary of South Indian daily life, from betel leaf to the pyol where neighbours sit and talk, is used without explanation, which is why Brians glosses it for American students. The irony is gentle: the holy man's authority is accidental, but the villagers' need is real.
historical_context: Published in 1958, eleven years after independence, by Viking in New York and Methuen in London. Narayan said that the episode of the reluctant holy man came from a real incident he had read about in a newspaper (Brians). The Sahitya Akademi, India's national academy of letters, gave it the first of its awards for English in 1960 (the Akademi's list; Contemporary Authors dates Narayan's award 1961).
literary_significance: The Narayan novel most widely read and adapted. Vijay Anand's Hindi film Guide (1965), with Dev Anand as Raju and Waheeda Rehman as Rosie, changed the ending; an English-language version written by Pearl S. Buck and directed by Tad Danielewski was screened at Cannes in 2007 (Wikipedia). Harvey Breit and Patricia Rinehart's stage adaptation was produced at the Hudson Theatre in New York in 1968 (Contemporary Authors), a production William Goldman profiled in The Season. In 2022 it was chosen for the Big Jubilee Read, a list of seventy books by Commonwealth authors.
bibliographical_notes: New York: Viking, 1958 (Contemporary Authors; first American edition, 220 pp., per Wikipedia); London: Methuen, 1958 (Wikipedia; Mondal). Stage adaptation by Harvey Breit and Patricia Rinehart (Hudson Theatre, New York, 1968); film, Guide (1965).
thematic_analysis: Imposture and transformation: Raju is a guide in successive senses, to tourists, to Rosie's career and at last to the villagers, and the question the novel leaves open is whether the pretended holy man becomes a real one; Brians notes that the book begins as a comic look at a rogue's life and 'evolves into something quite different'. Faith and its uses: the villagers' belief creates Raju's role, Velan's faith survives his confession, and the fast can be read either as the culmination of a fraud or as a genuine sacrifice; Brians cautions that Narayan was not a devout Hindu and objected to Westerners' assumption that all Indians are deeply spiritual. Art and commerce: Rosie's dancing, scorned by her husband, becomes under Raju's management a business, and Brians points to the double standing of the traditional temple dancer, of whom the novel offers both negative and positive images. Publicity: the fast turns into a spectacle reported by the press. Gale's encyclopedia stresses that Raju is unable to convince the villagers that he is a fraud.
summary: Raju, a popular and unscrupulous guide nicknamed 'Railway Raju', falls in love with Rosie, wife of the archaeologist Marco, while the couple visit Malgudi. When Marco abandons her, Rosie moves in with Raju, whose mother leaves the house; Raju becomes her manager and makes her a famous dancer, then grows controlling and is jailed for two years for forgery. Released, he shelters in an abandoned temple near the village of Mangal, where the villager Velan takes him for a sadhu; when drought brings famine, the villagers expect him to fast for rain, and the fast becomes a public spectacle.
critical_context: Anthony West, in the New Yorker in 1958, called it 'the best of R. K. Narayan's enchanting novels about the South Indian town of Malgudi and its people' and 'a profound statement of Indian realities' (quoted by Gale). Gale reports that it is usually considered his most accomplished novel, and Brians calls it 'one of his most interesting books'. Readers differ over the ending: Wikipedia stresses that Raju's fate is left to the reader, whereas Gale's summary has him die during the fast and be revered as a saint.
research_notes: Not read. The plot follows Wikipedia; the first of the three parts of Brians's study guide confirms the opening at the temple and the alternation of present and past. Gale's one-sentence summary places Raju's arrival in Malgudi and has him die and become a saint; both conflict with Wikipedia's fuller account and are not followed. Contemporary Authors and the Akademi's list disagree on the year of the award (1961 and 1960), and Contemporary Authors calls the 1968 production Off-Broadway, although the Hudson is a Broadway house (general knowledge) and Goldman's book is about Broadway.

title: The Man-Eater of Malgudi
description: A comic novel published by Viking in New York in 1961, in which Nataraj, a contented printer of Malgudi, has his press and his peace taken over by Vasu, a bullying taxidermist who moves into his attic. Wikipedia notes that Narayan draws on the myth of Bhasmasura, and Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia calls the novel 'another triumph' after The Guide.
plot_or_argument: Nataraj lives in a large ancestral house in Malgudi and runs a small printing press with one employee, Sastri; a poet and a journalist named Sen are among the friends who gather there. Vasu, a taxidermist come in search of the wildlife of the Mempi Hills, walks into the press demanding five hundred visiting cards, and soon installs himself in its attic, promising to stay only a few days. Nataraj and Sastri come to see him as a rakshasa, a demon. Vasu bullies away Nataraj's friends and customers, shoots a pet dog and many other animals and birds, poaches in the hills, fills the neighbourhood with the stench of his work and entertains women in the attic; when Nataraj questions him, Vasu complains to the rent controller as a harassed tenant. As Nataraj's poet friend prepares a celebration for the release of his book of verse on Krishna, Rangi, a temple dancer, tells Nataraj that Vasu means to kill Kumar, an elephant Nataraj has brought from the hills for treatment as a favour to a friend. Muthu, a tea-shop owner, agrees to help, but Nataraj fails to stop Vasu; resolving on a final confrontation, he finds him asleep, and next morning Vasu is dead. The autopsy finds a blow from a blunt weapon; the case is closed, but Nataraj's press is ruined and his friends avoid him. Later he learns through Sastri, who heard it from Rangi, that Vasu died when he brought his own powerful hand down on a mosquito sitting on his head. The story ends with the moral that demons bring about their own destruction.
narrative_structure: A chronological narrative told by Nataraj (his first-person narration is general knowledge), building from Vasu's arrival to the night of the celebration and closing with the revelation of how he died.
principal_characters: Nataraj; Vasu; Sastri; Sen; the poet; Rangi; Muthu; Kumar (an elephant)
meter_and_prosody: A comedy of mounting exasperation; Vasu's brute vitality is set against Nataraj's timidity, and the climax turns a mythic pattern into farce.
historical_context: Published by Viking in 1961, three years after The Guide, and set in Malgudi and the Mempi Hills. Narayan's own retellings of Indian myths, Gods, Demons, and Others, followed in 1964 (Contemporary Authors).
literary_significance: Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia calls it 'another triumph' after The Guide and lists it among Narayan's major works. It sets a Hindu myth inside a realistic Malgudi story, as Wikipedia observes, and its cast of printer, poet, journalist, temple dancer and tea-shop owner shows the cross-section of the town that the novels assemble.
bibliographical_notes: New York: Viking, 1961; 250 pp. (Contemporary Authors; Wikipedia). The London edition was not checked.
thematic_analysis: Good and evil in a comic key: Vasu is a modern rakshasa, and his death enacts the legend of Bhasmasura, the demon who could turn to ashes anyone on whose head he laid his hand and who was tricked into laying it on his own (Wikipedia names the myth; its content is general knowledge). Hospitality and its abuse: Nataraj's inability to refuse or expel his guest is both a virtue and a weakness. Exploitation of nature: the slaughter of the hills' wildlife and the threat to the elephant. Community: the circle of printer, poet and journalist stands for a gentle town life that the bully disrupts.
summary: Vasu, a strongman and taxidermist come to hunt in the Mempi Hills, installs himself in Nataraj's attic, drives away his friends and customers, shoots animals for stuffing and plans to shoot an elephant Nataraj has brought down from the hills; he is found dead, having struck his own head while killing a mosquito.
research_notes: Not read; the plot follows Wikipedia. Nataraj's first-person narration and the content of the Bhasmasura legend are general knowledge.

title: The Vendor of Sweets
description: A novel published by Viking in New York and, as The Sweet-Vendor, by the Bodley Head in London in 1967. Jagan, a widowed sweet-seller of Malgudi and a lifelong Gandhian, struggles to understand his only son, Mali, who comes back from creative-writing studies in America with a companion, Grace, and a scheme to manufacture story-writing machines.
plot_or_argument: Jagan, fifty-five, sells sweets in Malgudi and prospers. In his youth he left his studies to follow Gandhi in the freedom struggle, was commended by Gandhi for wearing hand-spun cloth, and he still lives by the Bhagavad Gita and by naturopathy, on which he has written a book that has lain at Nataraj's press for five years. His wife, Ambika, died of a brain tumour, leaving him to bring up their son, Mali, whom he spoils. In college Mali announces that he wants to be a writer and, without telling his father, arranges to go to America to study creative writing, using money from the cash Jagan has hidden from the tax collector. Jagan accepts this and proudly shows Mali's letters to everyone. Years later Mali returns, Westernised, with Grace, half-American and half-Korean, whom he calls his wife; Jagan grows fond of her and feels that Mali neglects her. Mali's grand scheme, a factory for story-writing machines with unnamed American partners, needs his father's money, and Jagan's refusal deepens the rift. Troubled, Jagan withdraws from the shop; a meeting with an eccentric 'bearded man', whose eloquence makes him reflect on his monotonous life, stirs a longing for renunciation and memories of his married years. When Mali is arrested for drunken driving and deserts Grace, Jagan tells his cousin that a dose of prison life will do him no harm, but writes a cheque for the preliminary costs of his bail and offers to buy Grace a ticket home if she wants one.
narrative_structure: A third-person narrative centred on Jagan, moving between the present and his memories of youth, marriage and Gandhi; Wikipedia calls the book the 'biography' of its fictional sweet-vendor.
principal_characters: Jagan; Mali; Grace; Ambika; Jagan's cousin; the bearded man
meter_and_prosody: Gentle irony at Jagan's expense: his maxim 'Conquer taste, and you will have conquered the self' (Wikipedia) sits beside his trade in sweets, and his piety beside his concealed cash.
historical_context: Published in 1967, with the British edition retitled The Sweet-Vendor (Contemporary Authors). Its contrast between a Gandhian of the freedom-struggle generation and a son formed by America sets the clash of generations in post-independence India. It was adapted as 'Mithaivalla' for the Hindi television series Malgudi Days (Wikipedia).
literary_significance: Wikipedia makes the generation gap its main theme and the clash of Indian and Western culture another. Critics have read it beside The Financial Expert as a novel of fathers (Contemporary Literary Criticism extract) and with The English Teacher and The Financial Expert for its symbols (G. S. Amur, via eNotes).
bibliographical_notes: New York: Viking, 1967; London: Bodley Head, 1967, as The Sweet-Vendor (Contemporary Authors).
thematic_analysis: Fathers and sons and the generation gap, which Wikipedia calls the main theme, and which the excerpt in Contemporary Literary Criticism pairs with The Financial Expert as novels told from the father's side. Tradition and the West: Jagan's Gandhian austerity, his Gita and his naturopathy against Mali's American ambitions and his claim that Grace is his wife. Money and conscience: Jagan's hidden, untaxed cash sits uneasily with his Gandhian virtue, and Wikipedia's character note says he uses religion to quiet his agitation. Renunciation: the ending turns to the Hindu ideal of withdrawal from worldly life.
summary: Jagan, fifty-five, prosperous and devoted to the Bhagavad Gita, naturopathy and hand-spun cloth, indulges his motherless son; Mali leaves college, goes to America with money taken from his father's hidden savings and returns with Grace and a business plan Jagan will not fund. Jagan drifts towards renunciation, and when Mali is arrested for drunken driving he leaves him to the law while paying towards his bail and offering Grace her fare home.
research_notes: Not read. The plot follows Wikipedia, whose article is flagged for more citations and cites a SuperSummary page for the paragraph on Jagan's background. Its description of the bearded man as a 'hairdryer' looks like a slip and is not used. Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia mentions 'two less popular works' between The Man-Eater of Malgudi and A Tiger for Malgudi without naming them; by Contemporary Authors' list they would be this novel and The Painter of Signs.

title: A Horse and Two Goats and Other Stories
description: A collection of short stories published by Viking in New York in 1970, named after one of Narayan's best-known stories, a comedy of misunderstanding between a poor old goatherd and an American visitor.
plot_or_argument: In the title story, as Contemporary Authors summarises it, Muni, a poor goatherd, rests in the shade of a statue of a horse made of clay while his goats graze. An American businessman passing by wants to buy the statue for his house in New York. Neither speaks the other's language, so the American assumes he is negotiating for the horse while Muni believes he is selling his goats. When the American hands him a hundred rupees, a vast sum for the old man, Muni runs home to tell his wife; the American hires a truck and carts the statue away, the goats wander home by themselves, and Muni is left to explain as best he can how he came by so much money. The sources consulted do not list the other stories in the volume.
narrative_structure: Built on a double dialogue in which each speaker develops 'his own hermetically-sealed interpretation of the other's words and gestures' (Crane).
meter_and_prosody: Comic irony and what Crane calls a 'wonderful double discourse'; the story's charm, he adds, lies in Narayan's refusal to pass judgment.
historical_context: Published in 1970 by Viking, Narayan's American publisher since The Guide. Narayan had described his own first journey to America, in 1956, in My Dateless Diary (1960); the title story reverses the direction, bringing an American to an Indian village.
literary_significance: With 'An Astrologer's Day', the title story is among Narayan's best-received (Contemporary Authors), and Crane's entry in the Reference Guide to Short Fiction treats it as a model comedy of cultural misunderstanding.
bibliographical_notes: New York: Viking, 1970 (Contemporary Authors). Contents and the London edition not checked.
thematic_analysis: Cross-cultural incomprehension; poverty and value, since each man prizes the clay horse differently; humour without judgement. Ralph J. Crane locates the irony in 'the total benign incomprehension that exists between the two' (Contemporary Authors).
summary: Headed by 'A Horse and Two Goats', in which Muni, an old goatherd, and an American businessman who wants to buy the clay horse beside which Muni rests bargain without a common language.
research_notes: Not read; contents other than the title story not identified.

title: The Painter of Signs
description: A short novel published by Viking in New York in 1976, with a London edition from Heinemann, in which Raman, a rationalist sign-painter of Malgudi, falls in love with Daisy, a young woman who runs the town's family-planning campaign, and loses her to her vocation.
plot_or_argument: Raman takes the craft of lettering seriously: his signboards, made of the best rosewood from the Mempi mountains, are better, he believes, than his rival Jayaraj's. He lives on Ellaman Street with his aunt, a conservative old woman fond of mythological stories and family gossip, whose interest in his doings irritates him and whom he feels guilty for neglecting. Not orthodox himself, he despises superstition and caste and reads old books on science and history, though he is given to quoting scripture. Daisy, an intense young woman working in family planning, hires him to make a signboard for her office; he is captivated by her precision, authority and devotion to her work, and accompanies her on a three-week tour of the villages around Malgudi to find sites for messages on population control. His resolve never to marry weakens. Daisy tells him about her complicated past and admits that she is attracted to him; they spend nights together and decide on a Gandharva marriage, the simplest form of union, on her terms: she will not change her name or keep house for him. His aunt, upset above all by his marrying outside his caste, asks him to arrange a one-way journey to Benares and goes despite his pleas. On the morning Daisy is to move into his house she changes her mind, fearing that married life will compromise her purpose and independence, and leaves Malgudi for a three-year family-planning project in villages across India, while Raman tells her that his house will be open to her whenever she returns.
narrative_structure: A narrative that follows Raman's point of view in Wikipedia's account, with Daisy's past told when she confides in him, ending without reconciliation.
meter_and_prosody: Comic irony at the expense of a rationalist who keeps quoting the scriptures, and of his infatuation with a woman who shuns every comfort (Wikipedia's account of the characters).
historical_context: Published in 1976. India's family-planning programme, which Daisy serves, became notorious for coercive sterilisation during the Emergency of 1975-1977 (general historical knowledge). Richard Cronin's essay reads the novel with Waiting for the Mahatma to examine V. S. Naipaul's view of the religious and the political in Narayan (eNotes).
literary_significance: Daisy belongs with Narayan's independent women, whom the women's studies article groups with Rosie of The Guide and Shanti of Mr. Sampath. It was reprinted in The World of Malgudi (2000), an omnibus of four novels (Contemporary Authors).
bibliographical_notes: New York: Viking, 1976 (Contemporary Authors); London: Heinemann (Wikipedia; year not checked). The American jacket is by Abner Graboff (Wikipedia).
thematic_analysis: Love against vocation: Daisy, who in the women's studies article asserts her autonomy by refusing motherhood along with other conditions, chooses her work over marriage. Modernity and tradition: Raman's rationalism and his love across caste set against his aunt's orthodoxy and her retreat to Benares. The state in the village: Daisy's campaign brings the government's population policy into Malgudi's countryside. Art as craft: Raman's pride in his lettering.
summary: Raman, who lives with his pious aunt and prides himself on his lettering, paints boards for Daisy's family-planning office and tours the villages with her; they become lovers and plan a simple marriage, his aunt leaves for Benares rather than see him marry outside his caste, and on the day Daisy is to move in she leaves for a three-year campaign elsewhere in India.
research_notes: Not read. Wikipedia's plot section is flagged as unreferenced; it agrees with the women's studies article (a search extract) on Daisy's refusals. Gale's 'two less popular works' (see The Vendor of Sweets) would include this novel.

title: A Tiger for Malgudi
description: A novel narrated by a tiger, published in 1983 by Viking in New York and Heinemann in London. Raja, old and in a zoo, tells of his life in the jungle, his capture and training in a Malgudi circus, his rampage, and his taming by a holy man, the Master, with whom he finds peace. Narayan's introduction traces the idea to a report he read of a monk moving about with a pet tiger at the Kumbh Mela in Allahabad.
plot_or_argument: Raja, an old tiger in a zoo, tells his own story. Young and free in the jungle, he mated with a tigress and raised a litter until hunters killed his whole family. He took revenge on the cattle and livestock of nearby villages until poachers caught him and sent him to a circus in Malgudi, where a harsh trainer known only as the Captain, owner of the Grand Malgudi Circus, starved him and forced him to perform. He lived in captivity for some time, but his wild instincts overcame him and he mauled and killed the Captain. After a long rampage through the town he was taken, this time willingly, by a monk, the Master, who befriended him and with whom he found peace in the hills. Sensing his own end approaching, the Master gave the ageing tiger to the zoo, where he is cared for and admired, and where, watched by children, he realises that he has done something to make people happy. Wikipedia's cast list adds the Captain's wife, Rita; Madan, a film producer and director; Jaggu, an actor; Alphonso, a hunter and poacher; and Jayaraj, a frame-maker.
narrative_structure: A retrospective first-person narrative by the tiger, preceded by Narayan's introduction on its origins; it moves from jungle to circus, town and hermitage and ends in the zoo.
principal_characters: Raja (the tiger); the Captain; Rita; Madan; Jaggu; Alphonso; the Master; Jayaraj
meter_and_prosody: Narayan's plain style adapted to an animal narrator, whose view of human customs produces irony; Wikipedia says he consulted the tiger expert K. Ullas Karanth (an unreferenced statement).
historical_context: Published in 1983, when Narayan was in his late seventies. His introduction names three prompts: a report of a monk moving around with a pet tiger at the Kumbh Mela, accounts of lasting friendships between tigers and people, and a bookmark showing a tiger with the words 'I'd love to get into a good book' (Wikipedia, citing S. R. Ramteke, 1998, and the 1995 Allied edition).
literary_significance: Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia says that, with a tiger as its protagonist, it 'made yet another impression', but that it was the last Narayan novel to receive wide critical attention, with mixed reviews and a few critics' disappointment. It was reviewed by Phoebe-Lou Adams in the Atlantic and in People (Contemporary Authors), and later reprinted in The World of Malgudi (2000).
bibliographical_notes: New York: Viking, 1983 (Contemporary Authors); London: Heinemann, 1983 (Wikipedia); 175 pp.
thematic_analysis: Captivity and freedom; the bond between a wild creature and a renunciant, which Wikipedia singles out as the book's moving centre; violence and its taming; and detachment, which Wikipedia relates to the teaching of the Buddha's enlightenment. Human cruelty, in the hunters, poachers and the Captain, is seen from the animal's side.
summary: Raja loses his tigress and cubs to hunters, raids village livestock, is caught by poachers and sold to a circus in Malgudi, where the Captain starves and trains him; he kills the Captain and runs loose in the town until the Master calms him and takes him to the hills, later giving him to the zoo.
research_notes: Not read; the plot follows Wikipedia. Karanth's part is unreferenced there. Gale calls it Narayan's twelfth novel, which matches Contemporary Authors' list.

title: Talkative Man
description: A short novel narrated by a Malgudi man known as the Talkative Man, published by Heinemann in London in 1986 and by Viking in New York in 1987; Kirkus called it 'really a long short story'.
plot_or_argument: The Talkative Man, a comfortable Malgudi resident who sends reports to the newspapers and earned his name, he says, because he 'cannot contain' himself, tells his story in a corner of the Boardless Hotel (Kirkus). In the library he meets an imposing stranger in a full suit, Dr. Rann, who says he comes from Timbuctoo and is engaged on a 'vital project' for the United Nations, and who eventually reveals that his work concerns a little weed that will eat up the world by the year 3000. Meanwhile a very large lady, an officer of the Home Guard in Delhi who carries a small pistol, holds the narrator for hours at the station with her story of faithless love: she is Rann's wife. The narrator must keep husband and wife apart and also prevent Rann's seduction of the librarian's granddaughter; after the tumult of Rann's public lecture a solution is found, and months later Mme Rann has the last word. A postscript by Narayan explains why he did not expand the story (Kirkus; Wikipedia).
narrative_structure: First-person narration by the Talkative Man, told in the Boardless Hotel (Kirkus), followed by an author's postscript.
principal_characters: The Talkative Man; Dr. Rann; Rann's wife; the librarian; the librarian's granddaughter
meter_and_prosody: Garrulous, comic storytelling; Kirkus compared it with Isaac Bashevis Singer's shtetl tales.
historical_context: The Talkative Man had narrated earlier Narayan stories (general knowledge); here he lives in Kabir Street, like the hero of the next novel, The World of Nagaraj (Mondal). Kirkus counted the book as the fifteenth Malgudi work.
literary_significance: A late, slight novel, but its narrator reappears in the cast of The World of Nagaraj (Wikipedia), and the women's studies article counts its Sarasa among Narayan's women who choose a career for themselves.
bibliographical_notes: London: Heinemann, 1986; New York: Viking, 1987 (Contemporary Authors; Wikipedia gives the 1987 Library of Congress call number). Wikipedia's infobox also shows an Indian edition from Indian Thought Publications. Kirkus gives Viking and 1 February 1986.
thematic_analysis: Imposture and the glamour of the foreign expert and his United Nations project; gossip and the compulsion to tell stories, embodied in the narrator; and the deserted wife's pursuit of her husband.
summary: The narrator's dealings with Dr. Rann, a smartly dressed stranger 'from Timbuctoo' who says he is working on a project for the United Nations, whose deserted wife comes looking for him, and whose courtship of the librarian's granddaughter the narrator tries to stop.
research_notes: Not read. Contemporary Authors (Viking, 1987) and Kirkus (Viking, 1 February 1986) disagree on the American date; a Los Angeles Daily News review of 15 March 1987 (cited by Wikipedia) supports 1987. Plot details found only in reader reviews and blogs are not used.

title: The World of Nagaraj
description: Narayan's fourteenth and last novel, published by Viking in New York in 1990. Nagaraj, a gentle, childless man of Kabir Street in Malgudi who keeps the books for a sari shop and has long planned a book on the sage Narada, finds his quiet life disturbed when his brother's wayward son, Tim, comes to live with him.
plot_or_argument: Nagaraj's world is comfortable. He lives in his family's spacious house in Kabir Street with his wife, Sita, and his widowed mother, fills his day with letter-writing, coffee and keeping the books for his friend Coomar's Boeing Sari Company, and sits on his verandah planning the book he means to write on the life of the sage Narada. A mild man from a well-to-do family, he has no children and has grown fond of his elder brother Gopu's son, christened Krishnaji but known as Tim. When Tim leaves his ambitious, land-owning father and comes to live with his uncle, Nagaraj is forced to take responsibility for him; puzzled by the young man's secret late-night activities and by the strong smell of spirits that lingers behind him, he finds his days filled with unwelcome complications that threaten the calm of his world (Wikipedia, paraphrasing a publisher's description). Malgudi figures pass through: Jayaraj the photographer, who sleeps on a bench outside his shop at the Market archway for fear his lens will be stolen and is woken every day by Nagaraj; Kanni the betel-seller; an old, absent-minded priest; Bari the stationer; a drunken engineer; and the Talkative Man. Contemporary Authors calls it the tale of an easygoing townsman bedevilled by 'the dual trials of caring for his wayward nephew and trying to write a book about an obscure Indian saint'.
narrative_structure: A comic narrative of domestic routine and its disruption; Mondal notes that it shares its pattern with Talkative Man, in which a comfortable Kabir Street man with literary ambitions has his peace disturbed by an outsider.
principal_characters: Nagaraj; Sita; Nagaraj's mother; Gopu; Tim (Krishnaji); Coomar; Jayaraj; Kanni; the Talkative Man
meter_and_prosody: Gentle comedy and irony; Hanif Kureishi praised its superb irony and said Narayan was 'in control of all his subtle effects' (Contemporary Authors).
historical_context: Published in 1990, when Narayan was eighty-three, as his last novel; Julian Moynahan's New York Times review called it his fourteenth. Narada, the wandering sage of Hindu myth who carries news between gods and men (general knowledge), gives Nagaraj his never-written subject.
literary_significance: In Moynahan's phrase, the latest building block in 'a shining edifice', it closes the sequence of Malgudi novels Narayan began in 1935. Kureishi, reviewing it in the Observer, called Narayan 'a master' and urged readers of 'long, tediously clever' novels to think of 'the wisdom and humour Narayan gently slips into his small but luminous masterpieces'; Publishers Weekly found the Malgudi residents 'talkative, philosophical and able to confront events with wonder and humor' (Contemporary Authors).
bibliographical_notes: New York: Viking, 1990 (Contemporary Authors). A London edition was reviewed in the Observer on 25 March 1990 but not identified; Penguin's paperback followed in 1991 (Wikipedia).
thematic_analysis: Ambition and inertia: Nagaraj's unwritten book on Narada is a comic image of the unrealised life, and Mondal links the mythical Narada, compelled to pass on tales and news, to the storyteller of these late novels. Family duty: the childless uncle's responsibility for a rebellious nephew, and the strain between brothers. Settled habit and the young: Tim's nights and drinking disturb a household of fixed routines. Community: the gallery of Kabir Street and market characters.
summary: Nagaraj lives with his wife Sita and widowed mother in the family house, keeps accounts for Coomar's Boeing Sari Company and plans his book on Narada; Tim, son of his ambitious brother Gopu, leaves home and moves in, and his late nights and the smell of spirits about him bring turmoil into the house.
research_notes: Not read. Wikipedia's article is a stub whose plot paraphrases a publisher's description; Contemporary Authors' one-sentence summary agrees. Tim's fate and the ending were not checked.
